definition.text: Obtaining the materials, products and services a company needs from suppliers in a way that is socially and environmentally responsible while still economically sound.

facts.text: Global supply chains and pressure to cut costs have harmed environments and communities, especially in developing nations, and awareness has grown since the 1990s.
A company is understood to be only as sustainable as the start of its supply chain.
Supply chains harm nature mainly through resource depletion and pollution, leading to biodiversity loss, habitat destruction and soil degradation.
Firms put it into practice through supplier codes of conduct, supplier selection and assessment, and supplier development.
It grew out of corporate social responsibility, which took on environmental duties in the 1990s with Elkington's triple bottom line.
Responsible sourcing means complying with ethical rules such as no child labour; sustainable sourcing goes further and acts to improve conditions.
The growing number of standards has raised costs for producers and caused confusion over their meaning and legitimacy.
It relates directly to Sustainable Development Goal 12, responsible consumption and production.

definition.text: Requirements on matters such as human rights, worker safety and environmental impact that producers, traders and retailers may be asked to meet, adopted voluntarily along the value chain.

facts.text: They arose as regulation of global business shifted from governments to private actors, with consumers holding companies to account.
They may be government-led, such as the USDA Organic label, or created by NGOs, such as FairTrade and Rainforest Alliance.
The FairTrade label aims to empower small producers mainly through a minimum price paid to them.
Many companies write their own standards instead, such as Starbucks' C.A.F.E. Practices.

definition.text: Partnerships of NGOs, companies, suppliers and governments that use voluntary, market-based approaches to make production of a particular product or sector more sustainable.

facts.text: They develop standards and issue certifications, and can also act as learning platforms.
Well-known examples include the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, the Forest Stewardship Council and the Better Cotton Initiative.
The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil awards a certified label to companies meeting criteria meant to limit palm oil's harm to people and the environment.

title: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
article: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures

definition.text: An international task force whose recommendations tell investors how companies are managing the risks of climate change and how they are governed.

facts.text: It was set up in December 2015 by the G20 and the Financial Stability Board, and was chaired by Michael Bloomberg.
Its recommendations cover four areas: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets.
It was formed partly in response to the 2015 Paris Agreement, whose national pledges were criticized for lacking transparent disclosure standards.
Its aim is to give investors, lenders and insurers the information they need to assess and price climate-related risks and opportunities.
It is described as the main framework used globally for climate disclosure in ESG.
Ahead of COP26 in 2021, the UK became the first G20 country to require 1,300 of its largest companies to disclose in line with it.
At COP26 the IFRS announced the International Sustainability Standards Board, into which the TCFD will converge.

notes: International body created by the G20 and FSB, not a single NGO; seeded in this chapter.
